title: Hard Cash: A Matter-of-Fact Romance
description: Published in 1863 and the most polemical of Reade's novels: a sensation plot built on the private lunatic asylum and on a stolen fortune, designed to expose the abuses of the English asylum trade.
plot_or_argument: Alfred Hardie, a young naval officer, is committed to a private asylum by his father's clerk on the word of a doctor who has been bribed; he escapes, recovers the money that has been stolen from his father, and rescues the heroine Julia Dodd from a similar conspiracy.
historical_context: The 1850s-60s, the private madhouse scandals, the Lunacy Commission, and the debate on wrongful confinement that produced the Lunacy Act of 1890.
literary_significance: Hard Cash is the central English novel of the private asylum scandal and the model of the documentary social novel: its evidence was drawn from parliamentary papers and court cases, and its publication helped to shape the public campaign against wrongful confinement.

title: It Is Never Too Late to Mend: A Matter-of-Fact Romance
description: Published in 1856 and Reade's first documentary novel: a triple narrative of the English prison system, the Australian goldfields and a rural seduction, designed to expose the cruelty of the separate system.
plot_or_argument: George Fielding emigrates to Australia for gold while his brother Tom is imprisoned for a crime he did not commit; the prison chapters record, with documentary fidelity, the treadmill, the crank and the silent system, and the novel ends with Tom's release and the brothers' prosperity.
historical_context: The 1850s, the separate system of prison discipline, the transportation system, and the Australian gold rush of 1851.
literary_significance: It Is Never Too Late to Mend is the most influential English novel of prison reform: its prison chapters were read as evidence in the contemporary debate and helped to end the separate system, and it established the method of documentary fiction that Reade and Zola would develop.

title: Cometh Up as a Flower
description: Published in 1867 and Broughton's sensational first novel: a first-person narrative of a woman who loves one man, marries another for money, and dies of the consequences.
plot_or_argument: Nellie Lestrange, a country clergyman's daughter, falls in love with Dick McGregor, but her family's poverty leads her to marry the wealthy Sir Digby Tempest; she is widowed, meets Dick again too late, and dies of consumption, telling her own story to the end.
historical_context: The 1860s, the marriage market, the 'Girl of the Period' controversy, and the circulating-library censorship of frank heroines.
literary_significance: Cometh Up as a Flower is one of the founding texts of the 1860s 'fast' novel: its heroine's unashamed desire and its refusal of a moral ending made it scandalous and made Broughton famous, and it is a key document in the pre-history of the New Woman novel.

title: Red as a Rose Is She
description: Published in 1870 and the best of Broughton's early novels: the story of a proud, passionate woman who refuses the man she loves and destroys herself by the refusal.
plot_or_argument: Blanche Bouverie, a wilful beauty, loves Captain Harry Glynn but rejects him in a fit of pride; she marries the elderly Lord Atherley, is widowed, and meets Glynn again when he is married to another woman; the novel ends with the two recognising what they have lost.
historical_context: The 1860s, the marriage market of the country house, and the code of feminine reticence that forbids a woman to speak first.
literary_significance: Red as a Rose Is She is Broughton's sharpest study of the costs of feminine pride, and one of the first English novels to analyse the convention that a woman must not declare her love.

title: Belinda. A Novel
description: Published in 1883 and the novel that made Broughton a satirist: a comedy of a widow's campaign to marry her daughter to a title, and of the young people who outwit her.
plot_or_argument: Belinda Churchill, a widow, sets out to secure a rich marriage for her daughter, and the courtship of the eligible Lord Robert and the clever Professor Forrester becomes a comedy of strategy, in which the older generation's ambition is defeated by the younger generation's honesty.
historical_context: The 1880s, the 'marriage market' and the peerage, the entry of women into university education, and the spread of divorce.
literary_significance: Belinda marks Broughton's turn from sensation to social comedy and is one of the first English novels to make the mother, rather than the daughter, the comic protagonist of the marriage plot.

title: Under Two Flags
description: Published in 1867 and the most popular of Ouida's novels: the story of a guardsman who takes the blame for a forgery, joins the French Foreign Legion, and wins glory in Algeria.
plot_or_argument: Bertie Cecil, the 'Beauty of the Brigades', shields a woman's honour by accepting disgrace; he enlists in the Chasseurs d'Afrique under the name Louis Victor, fights in the Sahara, is joined by his faithful Arab horse and his servant Rake, and is finally restored to his name and estate.
historical_context: The 1860s, the British army in the Crimea and India, the French conquest of Algeria, and the Victorian cult of the guardsman.
literary_significance: Under Two Flags was one of the best-selling English novels of the century and the model for the imperial adventure romance: its combination of military glamour, exotic North Africa and aristocratic honour shaped the popular literature of empire for two generations.

title: Moths
description: Published in 1880 and the most notorious of Ouida's society novels: the story of a beautiful, bored aristocrat married to a man she does not love, and of the cosmopolitan world that destroys her.
plot_or_argument: Vere Herbert, married to the brutal and much older Lord Jocelyn, is courted by the Russian prince Zouroff and the English diplomat Lord Dolly; the novel follows her through the great houses of London and Paris, and ends with her death and the ruin of the men who loved her.
historical_context: The 1870s, the 'fast' aristocratic set, the Prince of Wales's circle, and the circulating-library wars over the moral tone of fiction.
literary_significance: Moths was the most scandalous novel of 1880 and the clearest English example of the society novel as a critique of the aristocracy; its 'daring' was debated in the press and it shaped the picture of the 1870s haut monde for later readers.

title: A Dog of Flanders
description: Published in 1872 and one of the most beloved animal stories in the world: the tale of Nello, a poor Flemish boy, and his dog Patrasche, who dream of seeing Rubens's triptych in Antwerp cathedral.
plot_or_argument: Nello and Patrasche live with the old man Jehan Daas, haul milk to Antwerp, and are accused of a crime they did not commit; on Christmas Eve the boy and the dog walk to the cathedral, find it closed, and are found dead before the Rubens the next morning.
literary_form: Novella (in the collection A Leaf in the Storm, 1872)
historical_context: The 1870s, the Flemish peasant economy, the cult of Rubens, and the Victorian vogue for animal stories after Black Beauty.
literary_significance: A Dog of Flanders is one of the most widely translated animal stories ever written and the finest thing Ouida wrote: its fusion of art, poverty and animal devotion made it a permanent children's classic, and it is a key text in the Victorian literature of animals.

title: New Grub Street
description: Published in 1891 and the central English novel about the literary profession: the parallel stories of a scholar who cannot sell his work and a journalist who can sell anything.
plot_or_argument: Harold Biffen and Edwin Reardon struggle in the London of Grub Street: Reardon's serious novels fail, his marriage breaks down, and he dies in poverty, while Jasper Milvain, who writes for the market, prospers and marries Reardon's wife's friend. Biffen's realistic slum novel, Mr Bailey, Grocer, is published to no effect.
principal_characters: Edwin Reardon; Amy Reardon; Jasper Milvain; Harold Biffen; Alfred Yule; Marian Yule; John Yule; Maud Milvain; Dora Milvain; Whelpdale
historical_context: The 1880s, the collapse of the three-volume novel, the rise of the literary agent, the new mass periodicals, and the professionalisation of authorship.
literary_significance: New Grub Street is the founding English novel about the writer's market and one of the most exact records of literary life in the nineteenth century: its account of the economics of authorship has been the starting point for every subsequent discussion of the literary marketplace.

title: The Odd Women
description: Published in 1893 and the most important English novel of the 'surplus women' question: the story of three sisters, the plain women who must support themselves, and of two sisters' very different answers to their situation.
plot_or_argument: The Madden sisters, daughters of a ruined doctor, face a choice between genteel poverty and self-support: Alice and Virginia take poorly paid work as governesses and companions, while Monica, the beautiful one, marries the elderly and forbidding Edmund Widdowson and is destroyed by jealousy; the novel ends with Rhoda Nunn, the feminist who trains women for work, engaged to the cynical Everard Barfoot.
principal_characters: Rhoda Nunn; Monica Madden; Everard Barfoot; Edmund Widdowson; Mary Barfoot; Alice Madden; Virginia Madden; Micklethwaite
historical_context: The 1880s-90s, the 1891 census and the 'surplus' of half a million unmarried women, the expansion of women's clerical work, and the debate over marriage reform.
literary_significance: The Odd Women is the most rigorous English novel on the economic position of unmarried women and a founding text of English feminism: it treats marriage as an economic institution and asks what work and independence might mean, without either sentimentality or a happy ending.

title: The Nether World
description: Published in 1889 and the most documentary of Gissing's slum novels: the life of a Clerkenwell family in the 1880s, and the slow destruction of the young by the conditions they live in.
plot_or_argument: The Hewett household is watched over by the old grandfather, and the novel follows the fates of Clara, who becomes a servant and a kept woman, and Sidney Kirkwood, who marries Clara after the death of Jane Snowdon; the 'nether world' of the title is a whole society with its own economy, pleasures and desperations.
historical_context: The 1880s, the London slum and the charity organisations, the penny dreadful and the music hall, and the socialist movement of the 1880s.
literary_significance: The Nether World is the finest English novel of the London slum after Morrison and one of the most exact records of the 1880s poor: its refusal to sentimentalise made it a key text of English naturalism.

title: The Private Papers of Henry Ryecroft
description: Published in 1903 and Gissing's last completed book: the diary of a retired scholar who has escaped Grub Street into a cottage in Devon, and a meditation on literature, poverty and the consolations of a small income.
plot_or_argument: Ryecroft records the seasons, his reading, his memories of London and the Continent, his reflections on the English character and on the death of his friends; the book ends with his death and the quiet dispersal of his library.
historical_context: The 1900s, the Edwardian retreat from the city, the cult of the country cottage, and the professional writer's retirement.
literary_significance: The Private Papers of Henry Ryecroft was Gissing's most popular book and remains the classic English essay on the pleasures of modest leisure; it is the gentlest of his works and the one that best shows his prose at its most fastidious.

title: In the Year of Jubilee
description: Published in 1894 and Gissing's most ambitious study of the new generation of women: the story of Nancy Lord, a suburban girl who comes to London in the Jubilee year and is nearly destroyed by the pursuit of pleasure.
plot_or_argument: Nancy Lord, educated at a school for girls, drifts through the marriage market and becomes engaged to Luckworth Crewe, a vulgar speculator, and then to Lionel Tarrant, whom she secretly marries; the novel ends with her commitment to a marriage of duty and the care of her child after her lover's death.
historical_context: The 1887-97 years, the Jubilee, the new suburban London, the bicycle and the shop-girl, and the debate on the 'New Woman'.
literary_significance: In the Year of Jubilee is the sharpest English novel about the suburban girl of the 1890s and the most critical of the New Woman's pleasures; it is a key text for the study of gender, consumption and the city.

title: A Child of the Jago
description: Published in 1896 and the most famous English slum novel of the 1890s: the childhood and death of Dicky Perrott in the Old Jago, a handful of courts in Bethnal Green.
plot_or_argument: Dicky Perrott grows up in the Jago, steals, is sent to prison, tries to go straight, and is killed by a gang at the age of seventeen; the novel's exact record of the rents, trades, shops and fights of the district is its argument.
principal_characters: Dicky Perrott; Old Perrott; Hannah Perrott; Josh Perrott; Father Sturt; Bill Rann; Aaron Weech; Sally Green; Looey
historical_context: The 1890s, the East End of London, the closing of the Old Nichol slum in 1891-95 (the model for the Jago), and the debate between philanthropy and environmental determinism.
literary_significance: A Child of the Jago is the central English slum novel of the 1890s and the most influential text in the transition from the Victorian social-problem novel to modern working-class fiction; its controversy over heredity and environment made it a reference point for the sociology of poverty.

title: Tales of Mean Streets
description: Published in 1894 and Morrison's first book: fifteen sketches and stories of the East End, written in a hard, laconic prose and without a trace of charity or sentiment.
plot_or_argument: The stories move from the comic ('The Red Cow Group', a futile strike) to the terrible ('On the Stairs', a mother's death; 'Lizerunt', the destruction of a woman by her husband), and the volume ends with 'To Bow Bridge', a walk taken after a funeral.
historical_context: The 1890s, the East End, the new journalism and the 'cosmopolitan' short story, and the debate on the authenticity of slum writing.
literary_significance: Tales of Mean Streets is the finest English collection of slum stories and a founding text of the modern English short story: Kipling, Conrad and Wells all admired it, and its refusal of pity and moral commentary was a decisive break with Dickensian philanthropy.

title: Martin Hewitt, Investigator
description: Published in 1894 and the second great English detective series of the 1890s: the cases of Martin Hewitt, a professional investigator who works with Scotland Yard rather than against it.
plot_or_argument: Hewitt, a former journalist who employs a retired policeman as his assistant, solves cases of stolen documents, disguised swindlers, a case of mistaken identity and a locked-room problem, and the solutions turn on close observation and institutional knowledge rather than genius.
historical_context: The 1890s, the expansion of the Strand Magazine, the new professional detective and the police detective service.
literary_significance: Martin Hewitt is the most important English rival to Sherlock Holmes and the founding figure of the 'professional' detective: Morrison's series established the model of the investigator as a working professional that the twentieth-century detective story would develop.

title: The Hole in the Wall
description: Published in 1902 and Morrison's best late novel: a murder mystery set in the London docks, told by the child who saw the crime through a hole in a warehouse wall.
plot_or_argument: The orphan Stephen Blay is brought up by his grandfather, a Thames waterman, and witnesses the murder of a ship's captain in a dock warehouse; the investigation by his grandfather and the police uncovers a conspiracy of forgery and smuggling, and the novel ends with the child's testimony in court.
historical_context: The 1900s, the Port of London and its river trades, the London docks and their casual labour, and the child witness in the English courts.
literary_significance: The Hole in the Wall is one of the finest English novels of the Thames and the docks, and a key example of the child's-eye detective narrative that would be developed by Dickens's and Stevenson's successors.

title: Illustrations of Political Economy
description: Published monthly from February 1832 to 1834 and Martineau's first great success: twenty-five fictional case studies designed to teach the principles of political economy to ordinary readers through stories of wages, prices, population and the poor law.
plot_or_argument: Each tale takes a single economic principle and shows its working in the life of a family or a village: 'The Hill and the Valley' on capital and labour, 'A Manchester Strike' on combinations, 'Weal and Woe in Garveloch' on population, 'The Parish' on the new poor law.
literary_form: Series of twenty-five tales in monthly parts
historical_context: The 1830s, the Reform Act and the new political economy of Malthus and Ricardo, the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, and the mechanics' institute movement.
literary_significance: The Illustrations made political economy a popular literature: they sold tens of thousands of copies, were translated across Europe, and invented the fictional case study as a form of public education — the direct ancestor of the social-problem novel and of the documentary tradition.

title: Society in America
description: Published in 1837 after a two-year tour and the most systematic English account of the United States before Tocqueville's English readership: a study of American politics, religion, education, class, family life and slavery.
plot_or_argument: Martineau examines the machinery of American democracy — the constitution, parties, the press, the churches, colleges, commerce — and tests it against the condition of women, the treatment of the black population and the state of the poor, concluding that the country has failed its own principles in each case.
historical_context: The 1830s, Jacksonian democracy, the abolitionist movement and the mob violence of 1835, and the 'woman question' in America.
literary_significance: Society in America founded the comparative sociology of the United States and is the most important English book about American society between Birkbeck and Bryce; its chapters on the 'non-existence' of women and on slavery were used by the American feminist and abolitionist movements.

title: Deerbrook
description: Published in 1839 and Martineau's finest novel: the life of two sisters in a provincial town, and a study of middle-class English society, courtship and professional ambition.
plot_or_argument: Hester and Margaret Ibbotson come to live at Deerbrook with their aunt; Hester marries the surgeon Edward Hope, Margaret is loved by the misanthropic Mr Grey, and the novel follows the small society of the town through gossip, jealousy, illness and the death of the doctor.
principal_characters: Hester Ibbotson; Margaret Ibbotson; Edward Hope; Mr Grey; Mrs Enderby; Philip Enderby; Maria Young; Morris the surgeon
historical_context: The 1830s, the provincial town and its dissenting chapel, the medical profession, and the position of unmarried women.
literary_significance: Deerbrook is the most accomplished English provincial novel before Middlemarch and one of the first novels to treat the social life of a town as a subject in its own right; its picture of the gossip and mutual surveillance of village society is a landmark of English realism.

title: The Hour and the Man: A Historical Romance
description: Published in 1841 and the first English novel to take a black revolutionary as its hero: a fictional life of Toussaint Louverture and the Haitian revolution.
plot_or_argument: Toussaint, the former slave who becomes the leader of the revolution in Saint-Domingue, is shown in council, in battle and in his household, and the novel follows the uprising, the French expedition of 1802 and Toussaint's betrayal and death in the prison of Fort de Joux.
historical_context: The 1790s, the Haitian revolution, the abolitionist movement of the 1830s-40s, and the British emancipation of 1833.
literary_significance: The Hour and the Man is the founding English novel of the Haitian revolution and the first substantial fictional treatment of a black leader in English literature; it was read by abolitionists on both sides of the Atlantic and marks the limit of what a British novelist in 1841 could say about slave revolution.

title: Life in the Sick-Room: Essays
description: Published in 1844 and written out of Martineau's own long illness: a series of essays on the experience of invalidism, which she treats as a condition with its own duties, liberties and spiritual possibilities.
plot_or_argument: The essays address the sick person's relation to visitors, to doctors, to religion and to the world outside the sickroom; they attack the 'theology of consolation' that treats illness as a punishment and argue for the invalid's authority over her own life.
historical_context: The 1840s, the Victorian sickroom, the doctrine of resignation, and Martineau's own case (a uterine tumour and, later, deafness and heart disease).
literary_significance: Life in the Sick-Room is the founding English text of the literature of illness: it invented the first-person essay on being ill as a subject, and its arguments against the consolations offered to invalids were taken up by later feminist and disability writing.

title: Autobiography of Harriet Martineau
description: Written from the 1850s and published after her death in 1877, with a memorial by Maria Weston Chapman: one of the greatest Victorian autobiographies, and a completely unsentimental account of a working literary life.
plot_or_argument: Martineau recounts her Unitarian upbringing, the loss of her fortune, her deafness, her career, her American journey, her religious doubts, her mesmeric illness and her old age, and gives exact and often devastating verdicts on the public figures she knew.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Victorian life-writing tradition, and the posthumous publication arranged by her friend Maria Weston Chapman.
literary_significance: Martineau's Autobiography is the classic Victorian record of a woman's professional self-making and a model of unsentimental self-analysis; its judgments on her contemporaries make it a primary source for the literary history of the period.

title: 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors': Is the Classification Sound?
description: Published in Fraser's Magazine in December 1868 and the most effective single piece of Victorian feminist polemic: an argument against the legal classification of married women with criminals, idiots and minors.
plot_or_argument: Cobbe takes the legal doctrine of coverture and reads it literally: the married woman can make no contract, hold no property, sue no one and be sued by no one, exactly like the lunatic and the infant; she demonstrates the consequences through cases of deserted and abused wives and demands the reform of the law.
historical_context: The 1868 debate on the Married Women's Property Bill, the doctrine of coverture, and the case of the deserted wife.
literary_significance: 'Criminals, Idiots, Women and Minors' is one of the founding documents of English feminism and gave the campaign for the Married Women's Property Acts its most memorable argument; the essay is still the standard short statement of the legal position of the Victorian wife.

title: 'Wife-Torture in England'
description: Published in the Contemporary Review in 1878 and the most important Victorian essay on domestic violence: a documented account of wife-beating in England, with cases from the police courts and the assizes.
plot_or_argument: Cobbe collects the evidence of the courts over several years, shows that wife-beating is treated as a trivial offence, argues that the law's reluctance reflects the doctrine of the wife's submission, and proposes the flogging of convicted wife-beaters — a proposal she defends against the objections of her own allies.
historical_context: The 1870s, the campaign that produced the Matrimonial Causes Act amendment of 1878, the police courts, and the debate over corporal punishment.
literary_significance: 'Wife-Torture in England' created the public vocabulary for domestic violence and was directly responsible for the 1878 legislation that allowed magistrates to separate battered wives from their husbands; it is the founding text of the English literature on domestic abuse.
